title: The Vessel That Wouldn't Loosen
synopsis: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks arrives with elevated blood pressure and a racing pulse. The workup rules out preeclampsia, but the story of gestational hypertension unfolds — a placenta sending chemical signals that clamp down every vessel in her body.

chapters.heading: Scene 1 — With the patient
chapters.body: She walks into triage holding her belly, her face tight with worry. The nurse takes vitals and notes a heart rate of 120 and a blood pressure of 133 over 86 — not yet severe, but elevated for a woman at 24 weeks. Her breathing is quick, 23 breaths a minute, though her oxygen saturation stays at 100%. She sits down slowly, one hand on the armrest, and says she feels fine except for a mild headache that comes and goes.
chapters.visualHint: Medium close-up of the woman sitting on the exam table, one hand resting on her pregnant belly, the other gripping the edge of the mattress. Her bare feet are visible at the bottom of the frame.

chapters.heading: Scene 2 — With the attending
chapters.body: Dr. Oppong enters and sits across from her. He explains that her blood pressure is high for pregnancy and that the placenta may be sending signals that are tightening her blood vessels. He orders serial blood pressure checks, a urine test for protein, blood work to check her kidneys and liver, and a fetal ultrasound to make sure the baby is doing well.
chapters.visualHint: Wide three-quarter shot of Dr. Oppong seated, leaning forward, speaking to the patient. The fetal monitor is visible on the counter behind him.

chapters.heading: Scene 3 — Orders and data
chapters.body: The urine test comes back clean — no protein, no blood, no infection. The 24-hour urine protein is 150 milligrams, well below the 300-milligram threshold for preeclampsia. Her blood work is equally reassuring: creatinine 0.8, AST 22, platelets 283. The fetal ultrasound shows a normal heart rate and good movement. She has gestational hypertension, not preeclampsia.
chapters.visualHint: Close-up of the lab results printout on the counter, with the 24-hour urine protein value circled in pen. The patient's hand is visible in the foreground, resting on the paper.

chapters.heading: Scene 4 — Results land
chapters.body: Because her blood pressure is still above 140 over 90 on repeat checks, Dr. Oppong starts labetalol and nifedipine. The labetalol blocks catecholamines at the heart and vessels; the nifedipine directly relaxes the arteriolar smooth muscle. Together they tackle the hypertension from two angles. After the first dose, her blood pressure comes down to 148 over 92 — still elevated, but moving in the right direction.
chapters.visualHint: Medium shot of the nurse preparing the oral medications at the bedside. The patient is watching, her hands folded over her belly.

chapters.heading: Scene 5 — Treatment and mechanism
chapters.body: Dr. Oppong explains the mechanism: the placenta, needing more blood flow, sends chemical signals into the mother's circulation. Those signals cause widespread vasoconstriction — every vessel in her body clamps down. That's what drives the blood pressure up. The labetalol and nifedipine work by loosening that clamp. He also starts low-dose aspirin, 81 milligrams daily, to reduce the risk of preeclampsia developing over the coming weeks.
chapters.visualHint: Close-up of Dr. Oppong's hands holding a small white pill bottle of aspirin, with the patient's pregnant silhouette visible in the background against the curtain.

chapters.heading: Scene 6 — Plan together
chapters.body: She will go home on labetalol, nifedipine, and daily aspirin. She needs to check her blood pressure twice a day and return immediately if she develops a severe headache, vision changes, or right upper quadrant pain. Dr. Oppong schedules a follow-up in one week. She stands slowly, takes her prescription, and walks out — still holding her belly, but with her shoulders a little less tight.
chapters.visualHint: Wide shot of the patient walking toward the exit, one hand on her belly, the other holding the prescription paper. The nurse is at the desk in the background, writing notes.
